BEAST COACH

The Discipline Path

"Don't say I can't do it. Say I have not done it yet."

You don't need a meal plan or a training plan to fix this. Motivation fades no matter how good either one is. This program builds the one thing underneath both of them: the discipline to actually follow through. If you want to build your own meal ideas or a training sheet along the way, they're in here too, but they're the bonus, not the point.

What's Ahead

Everything below is locked until you reach it, on purpose. Here's the shape of the whole thing before you start:

  1. Identity Reset. You build proof you can trust yourself, one small habit at a time, over 30 days.
  2. Environment Reset. You remove the daily decisions that only exist to wear down your willpower.
  3. Social Playbook. You decide, ahead of time, how you'll handle the situations that actually get you.
  4. Routine Build. You build a week you can fall into on the days you don't feel like thinking.
  5. Reset Protocol. You decide your rule for a bad day, before you're in the middle of one.
  6. The Reminder. You choose something that keeps you honest, not something that tests you.
  7. Full System. Everything unlocks, meal ideas, a workout sheet, recipes, your targets, all optional.

You can move ahead if you like, but the aim of this is to do one step at a time. By the end of this full system, you should be ready to start your next journey: your new, exciting life of being healthy and happy.

Don't skip the Education section. Alongside the 7 steps, we've built in real tips, myths worth busting, and strategies that'll guide you through the next 60 days. It's unlocked the whole time, so dip into it whenever you want. Open the Education section →

Why This Exists

Here's something I've learned the hard way, more than once: the best meal plan, the most expensive coach, the best personal trainer, the best app for tracking every gram of everything, none of it matters if you don't have discipline. I've had access to all of it at different points and still ended up back at the start. Motivation got me going every time. It just never stuck around long enough to finish the job.

I started this more times than I can count, and gave up more times than I can count. For a while I assumed the problem was the plan, so I'd find a new one. Then I assumed it was the coach, so I'd find a new one of those too. Eventually I had to admit the plan was never the problem. If I was given a fit, athletic body once, through sheer motivation and a short burst of effort, I still didn't keep it, because I hadn't built anything underneath it to hold it up.

So I built this program for anyone in the same position, to build discipline first, before anything else. Looking back at what I actually did differently the time it worked, I didn't start with a diet and I didn't start with a training split. I started by building something I'm calling a discipline engine, a system that let me prove things to myself in small amounts until I could trust myself again. And once you trust yourself, everything else gets easier. It snowballs. Confidence stops being something you talk yourself into and starts being something you've already earned.

I also learned that going all in on day one is too much for your body and your mind to hold. You feel the shock of it almost immediately, and before you know it, you've quit again. So this time I started small. I began by just eating whole foods, nothing tracked, nothing restricted, as little friction as possible. Then every day, or every second day, I added one new thing. By the time thirty days had passed, it wasn't a list of rules I was forcing myself through anymore, it was just who I was. That's what this program is built to do for you.

— Stefan

BEFORE YOU START

The Psychology

This program works because it's built around how your brain actually sabotages you, not vague motivation advice. Below are the real mental blockers that derail people, and the fix for each one. Answer the question under each one honestly, in your own words. Nobody sees these but you, and they'll come back to you at the end, in your Full System summary, so you can see what you were thinking on day one.

1. Friction at Task Initiation

The "activation energy barrier" — why starting is the hardest part

Your brain picks comfort now over results later

This is why an abstract reward next month never beats the discomfort of starting today. The fix is to close the gap: pair the hard thing with something that feels good immediately (a podcast you only allow yourself during a workout, say), and track a visible streak the second you finish, so your brain gets paid on the spot.

What looks like laziness is usually avoidance

Procrastination is often an emotional defense against a task that makes you feel inadequate, confused, or dreadful, not a character flaw. The fix: before touching the task, spend 60 seconds naming the actual feeling ("tight chest, scared this will be bad"), then set a 5-minute timer and work through the discomfort without expecting it to feel good.

A vague starting point overwhelms you before you begin

"Work out for an hour" or "write the report" is too big and too fuzzy, so your brain stalls. Shrink the first move until there's zero resistance left: not "go to the gym," just "put your shoes on." Not "cook the meal," just "get the pan out."

2. Cognitive Depletion and the Willpower Fallacy

Willpower runs out by the evening — so stop relying on it

Every decision today drains the willpower you need tonight

By the time you're tired, there's nothing left for the hard calls. The fix is turning decisions into fixed rules ahead of time: the same meals, the same training slot, the same clothes, so nothing needs deciding when you're depleted.

Discipline isn't a feeling you wait for, it's a setup you build

If-then planning removes the willpower debate entirely by pre-deciding the response to a known trigger: "If I walk in the door from work, then I change into gym shoes before I sit on the couch."

Stress hands control to the part of your brain that wants the easy habit

Stress hormones switch off your rational brain and switch on automatic, high-dopamine coping habits, the ones you're trying to break. A standard 2-minute reset before you try to make a decision (two quick inhales through the nose, one long exhale through the mouth, or a splash of cold water on your face) calms that response down first.

3. Identity and Cognitive Distortions

What you believe about yourself decides whether the habit sticks

One slip doesn't ruin anything — treating it like it does, does

One off-plan meal or one missed session is a statistical blip, not a failure, but "all or nothing" thinking turns it into one anyway and you abandon the whole week. The rule: slipping once is an accident, slipping twice starts a new habit. And always keep a "floor", the bare minimum that still counts as showing up on a bad day.

You can't out-affirm an identity you don't have evidence for

Identity follows evidence, not pep talks. Every time you follow through on a small commitment, you're casting a vote for the kind of person who keeps their word to themselves. Enough votes and the identity becomes real.

Chasing the scale instead of the process burns you out at the first plateau

Outcomes like weight or visible progress move slowly and unevenly, so measuring success by them alone guarantees demotivation. Measure execution instead: how consistently you actually did the plan, as a percentage. Adherence is the win, independent of what the scale says that week.

4. Environmental and System Design Failures

Your environment is doing half the work, for or against you

Bad habits are one tap away, good habits take setup, that's backwards

Make the bad habit harder to reach: phone in another room, junk food out of the house. Make the good habit easier: gear, meals, and workspace prepped the night before, so tomorrow's version of you doesn't have to fight for it.

A perfect plan breaks at the first bad night of sleep

Build three tiers instead of one rigid plan. Ceiling: a full 10/10 day. Target: a solid, realistic 7/10 day. Floor: the bare minimum, maybe 10 push-ups and hitting your protein target. Dropping to the floor on a rough day is a planned, valid outcome, never a failure.

Without data, you'll always overestimate your effort and underestimate your lapses

A simple yes/no checklist beats a complicated tracker, because anything that takes more than 30 seconds a day gets abandoned. Keep it binary: did it happen or not.

STEP 1 OF 7

The Identity Reset

This is where it actually starts. Not with a diet, not with a gym program, with proof. For years I told myself I was someone who'd try and quit. What actually changed that wasn't one big decision, it was a hundred tiny ones stacking up until I couldn't argue with the evidence anymore.

— Stefan

Before you pick anything, read this. This is one of the most important parts of the whole program. Every day, come back here and add one habit, something you decide on yourself. It can be as small as making your bed every morning or being in bed by 8:30. Choose it carefully, because this is something you're committing to doing every single day from here on, not just once. You'll probably miss a day here or there, that's fine, aim for about 99%, not perfect. Add one new habit a day rather than several at once, that way it never becomes a massive shock all at once, it just quietly becomes who you are. Once you commit to a habit and write it down, you do it. By the end of 30 days you'll be most of the way there, and everything from Step 2 onward is built on top of what you've proven to yourself here.

    STEP 2 OF 7

    The Environment Reset

    This one might be one of the hardest things you do here, and also one of the most important. When I decided this was my last attempt, I didn't just decide it in my head, I went through my kitchen and physically removed what didn't belong in the life I was building. It wasn't just cleaning, it was closing a door on purpose.

    If there's something you can't throw away, kids' snacks, a partner's favourite treat, don't fight that. Put it somewhere separate instead, in the Goodbye Box below. This step isn't really about the food. It's about removing the daily decision so your future self doesn't have to rely on willpower for something that could've just been removed.

    — Stefan

    Don't treat this like a chore, treat it like a send-off. This is the moment you're closing the door on the old version of you, on purpose, so make it feel like it. Put music on. Film the clear-out, or grab a photo of the "before" pile on its way to the bin. If you're comfortable with it, post it, tag it, tell people what you're doing and why. You're not quietly tidying a kitchen, you're throwing yourself a goodbye party for a version of you that doesn't live here anymore.

    Built From Your Own Habits

    Some of what you logged in Step 1 needs something physically set up to actually work. Confirm those here.

    The Disposal Ritual

    Go through your kitchen now, and make an occasion of it. For each item below, tick it once it's actually done, not planned.

    One shelf for the household's trigger foods, one for yours, side by side.

    If you've got kids, or you live with people who aren't doing this with you, be honest with yourself: this is going to be a real struggle unless your willpower is already rock solid, and for most people it isn't yet, that's fine. You can't always just throw out the trigger foods when they belong to someone else too. If you genuinely can't remove something, don't pretend you will and then quietly fail. Instead, set up one dedicated shelf, in the fridge or the pantry, that's theirs, not yours. Everything that's a trigger for you lives on that shelf and nowhere else in the kitchen. You're not trying to control what everyone else eats, you're just making sure your own eyes and hands don't land on it by accident fifty times a day.

    The Goodbye Box

    For anything you're keeping, for someone else, not for you, write it a message and put it somewhere separate. If you're ever tempted to open that box, you have to read this again first.

    The Routine Build

    None of this works without a shape to fall into on the days you don't feel like it. My whole week changed once dinner stopped being a decision and started being a question of which meal I'd already made. Build yours below, it doesn't need to look like mine.

    — Stefan

    How this works: pick one day as your planning and shopping day, that's when you prep for the week ahead. Then go through each day below, one at a time, and set your wake time, training time, steps time, and target bedtime around your actual life, your job, your commute, your family, not an idealised version of it. If most weekdays look the same for you, build Monday properly then hit "Repeat this day for the rest of the week" instead of redoing it five times. The routine is the skeleton everything else hangs off, it's not optional just because you haven't started a meal plan or a training block yet. Showing up for wake time, steps, and bedtime on their own, every day, is still the habit that's actually being built here. Once you've saved it, print this page and put it somewhere you'll actually see it, on the fridge, the bathroom mirror, next to your bed, not filed away somewhere you'll forget to check.

    Your big planning and shopping day

    Build your week, one day at a time

    What meal planning are you doing this day?

    Shopping and Bulk Prep

    1. Buy protein in bulk, freeze in portions. Chicken breast, mince, and fish all freeze well, buy a week or two at once and portion it out.
    2. Repeat carbs on purpose. Rice, potatoes, and oats are cheap in bulk and boring enough that you won't be tempted to upgrade the meal.
    3. Shop from a list built before you walk in. Never from what looks good in the moment.
    4. Buy the same staples every week. A short, repeated shopping list is a feature, not a limitation.

    STEP 6 OF 7

    The Reminder, Not the Temptation

    When I did my kitchen reset, I had a six-pack of beer in the fridge. I tipped every can down the sink except one. That last one is still in there, probably well past its use-by date by now, and I haven't touched it. It's not there to test me, it's there to remind me. Every time I open that fridge I see it and I remember I chose this.

    Pick one thing like that for yourself, not a temptation, a reminder.

    A fair warning: this gets a lot harder if you're not eating enough. If you're under on protein or fibre for a few days, you'll be hungrier than you need to be, and that makes everything in this program feel unfair when it isn't. This step doesn't need a meal plan to work, but if you want to actually test yourself properly, it works a lot better once you're roughly hitting the protein, carbs, and fat targets from your profile.

    — Stefan

      ALWAYS OPEN

      Education

      This section isn't gated, read it whenever you want, before Step 1 or after Step 7, it doesn't matter. Nothing here asks anything of you. Most of what makes fat loss feel confusing isn't actually complicated, it's just surrounded by bad information. This is the real version: what's actually true about fat loss, what actually matters day to day, and the one thing most people never get told the full truth about, alcohol. Print it if you want something to keep.

      Part 1: The Top 20 Myths & Misconceptions About Fat Loss

      Part 2: 20 Core Educational Topics in Plain English

      Part 3: The Real Cost of Alcohol (It's Not Just the Liquid Calories)

      Most fitness guides warn you about alcohol by stating the obvious: "Beer has carbs," or "Cocktails are packed with sugar."

      While those empty calories matter, treating alcohol like simple liquid junk food misses the bigger picture. Alcohol doesn't just add calories to your day, it temporarily hijacks how your body processes energy, wrecks your internal chemistry, and sets off a multi-day domino effect that makes sticking to your routine uphill work.

      1. The Emergency Stop on Fat Burning

      Your body cannot store alcohol. Unlike protein, carbohydrates, or dietary fat, your body recognizes alcohol as a toxic substance that must be cleared out immediately.

      The moment alcohol enters your bloodstream, your liver stops everything else it was doing. Fat burning drops down to practically zero because your liver redirects its resources toward breaking down the alcohol and clearing it from your system.

      What happens to the food you eat while drinking? That burger, bowl of chips, or slice of pizza you eat while having a drink is not used for immediate energy. Because the furnace is busy clearing alcohol, nearly all the dietary fats and carbs from your food get shuttled directly into storage. Even after alcohol leaves your bloodstream, your liver spends hours recovering, keeping normal fat metabolism slowed down long after your last drink.

      2. The Blood Sugar Rollercoaster and Late-Night Cravings

      Ever notice that you never crave grilled chicken and steamed greens after a few drinks? While your liver is busy processing alcohol, it stops releasing steady glucose into your blood. This triggers a sharp drop in blood sugar levels.

      Your brain registers that drop as an energy crisis, triggering urgent cravings for fast, calorie-dense foods, usually greasy, refined carbohydrates. At the exact same time, alcohol dulls your prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that manages self-control and decision-making.

      You end up in a compromised spot: strong biological cravings paired with weakened impulse control. That is how a planned single drink turns into late-night snacking or ordering greasy food.

      3. The "Fake Sleep" Problem

      Many people drink a glass of wine or a beer to relax because it helps them pass out quickly. But alcohol is a sedative, not a sleep aid. Falling unconscious is very different from getting restorative sleep.

      Alcohol fragments your deep sleep and REM cycles, the critical stages where muscles recover, the brain clears waste, and metabolism resets. It raises your resting heart rate and elevates stress hormones while you are in bed. You wake up having spent eight hours in bed, but biologically running on the recovery of three broken hours.

      4. The Next-Day Hangover Effect: The Hidden Domino

      The real problem with alcohol rarely stops on the night you drink; it spills over into the next 24 to 48 hours. When you wake up dehydrated and under-recovered:

      1. Hunger signals run wild. Your body increases the hormone that drives appetite and suppresses the signal that tells you you are full.
      2. Daily movement tanks. You sit more, skip your walk, and avoid physical tasks because your brain is sluggish and looking for easy rest.
      3. Workouts lose quality. Even if you force yourself to train, strength, coordination, and endurance are compromised. You burn fewer calories, lift lighter weights, and increase your injury risk.
      4. The "Screw It" mindset takes over. Dehydration and low mental energy make cooking and meal prep feel overwhelming. Grabbing fast food feels like the easiest way through the day, turning one evening of drinks into a weekend-long setback.

      The bottom line: you don't need to give up socializing entirely. But view alcohol clearly for what it actually is, a metabolic pause button paired with a tax on your discipline. When you choose to drink, you're not just adding calories, you're pressing pause on your body's fat-burning systems for hours, and making the next day significantly harder on your energy, willpower, and nutrition. If fat loss is your main focus right now, protect your momentum: swap the regular evening drink for sparkling water, keep alcohol for intentional occasions, and don't let a few drinks derail several days of solid progress.
